items: Give the battery an equalizing charge whenever necessary.

Whenever the battery is subjected to discharge of more than 5 to10 
 percent of its rated capacity, it should be recharged as soon as possible.

Healthy cells, when fully charged, show a marked contrast between the 
 dark brown positive and the light grey negative plats.

For cells in transparent jars (SMF, SMBF, SMZA, SD, SDH, SGL, SGH), it is 
 extremely use full to inspect the appearance of each cell in the battery at 
 regular intervals.

Any cells not showing a healthy plate coloration, or having a specific 
 gravity or voltage noticeable lower than the other cells, or in which the 
 plates bubble unevenly or not at all, should be regarded as suspect.

Such cells should be carefully examined for internal short- circuits, 
 such as may be caused by small pieces of scale bridging across the plates.

A period of charging will normally restore such cells to the condition of 
 the remainder of the battery, but if it does not, expert advice should be 
 obtained immediately form FIAMM.

For regular monitoring of the battery condition select one cell near the 
 middle of the battery as a" pilot" cell (for batteries comprising more than 60 
 cells, select one pilot cell for every 60 cells).

The electrolyte specific gravity of the pilot cell ( s ) will be 
 indicative of the state of charge of the whole battery.

Notes:
When cells are supplied filled with acid they must be placed on float charge 
 or given an equalizing or freshening charge within 90 days from the date of 
 shipment.
Never add acid to increase specific gravity readings.
Gases given off by batteries on charge are explosive!
Don't smoke or permit open flames near batteries or do anything to cause 
 sparks.
The room in which the battery is installed should be well ventilated and its 
 temperature as moderate as the climate will allow.
The temperature of the electrolyte should preferably never exceed 38oC.
Procedures
Check the electrolyte levels in all cells regularly and if necessary top up 
 with distilled water.
Never allow the electrolyte level to fall below the "MIN" line.
Don't over fill the cells.
Set the charger to "equalize" for about 30 minutes to help mix the electrolyte 
 when water has been add.
Keep the battery and surroundings clean and dry.
Wipe the cells with a clean soft cloth dampened with clean water.
If necessary, a small amount of mild detergent may be added to the cleaning 
 water to remove any greasy film.
Don't use any special powders or solvents for cleaning the battery cells, as 
 scratching or damage to the plastic could occur.
Make sure that bolted connections are tight.
Keep connectors, posts and bolted connections covered with "No oxide" grease 
 for protection against corrosion.
Should any corrosion of the connections occur because of spilled acid ete.
Carefully remove corrosion materials, thoroughly clean and neutralize with 
 dilute ammonia or backing soda.
Dry the parts before coating them "No- oxide" grease to protect from further 
 corrosion.
Don't let the neutralizing solution enter the cell.
Keep the battery at the recommended charge voltage.

Give the battery an equalizing charge whenever necessary.
Whenever the battery is subjected to discharge of more than 5 to10 
 percent of its rated capacity, it should be recharged as soon as possible.
Cell Appearance
Healthy cells, when fully charged, show a marked contrast between the 
 dark brown positive and the light grey negative plats.
For cells in transparent jars (SMF, SMBF, SMZA, SD, SDH, SGL, SGH), it is 
 extremely use full to inspect the appearance of each cell in the battery at 
 regular intervals.
Any cells not showing a healthy plate coloration, or having a specific 
 gravity or voltage noticeable lower than the other cells, or in which the 
 plates bubble unevenly or not at all, should be regarded as suspect.
Such cells should be carefully examined for internal short- circuits, 
 such as may be caused by small pieces of scale bridging across the plates.
A period of charging will normally restore such cells to the condition of 
 the remainder of the battery, but if it does not, expert advice should be 
 obtained immediately form FIAMM.
Pilot Cell
For regular monitoring of the battery condition select one cell near the 
 middle of the battery as a" pilot" cell (for batteries comprising more than 60 
 cells, select one pilot cell for every 60 cells).
The electrolyte specific gravity of the pilot cell ( s ) will be 
 indicative of the state of charge of the whole battery.
Maintenance Record Data Sheet
Written records should be kept of battery maintenance, so that long-term 
 changes in battery condition may be monitored.
The following 
 Inspection Procedures are Recommended
Weekly
Check and record the overall float voltage at the battery terminals (not 
 at the charge!), and measure the pilot cell voltage.
Monthly
Record the battery voltage and the voltage, specific gravity and the 
 temperature of the pilot cell (s).
Quarterly (every 3 months)
Record the voltage, specific gravity and temperature of all cells.

It is a good practice to give the battery a full discharge test at 5 year 
 intervals until signs of degradation are observed or until the battery has 
 reached 85 percent of its original capacity
Once this stage has been reached, yearly capacity tests should be 
 conducted until the battery reaches the end of its useful life.
See IEEE standard 450-1980 for recommendations concerning test procedures 
 and battery replacement criteria.
